assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Peripheral thermoreceptors
items.clue: Sensory cells in the skin that detect its temperature.

items.label: Shivering
items.clue: Rapid, involuntary muscle contractions that release heat.

items.label: Thyroxin
items.clue: A hormone that raises the metabolic rate of most body cells.

items.label: Type 1 diabetes
items.clue: Beta cells of the pancreas are destroyed by the immune system.

questions.stem: What is the physiological change that underlies type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Beta cells are destroyed by the immune system.
Beta cells are damaged by dietary sugar.
Insulin in the blood stops digesting glucose.
Target cells respond less to insulin.

questions.explanation: In type 2 diabetes insulin is secreted, at least in the early years, but liver, muscle and adipose cells have become insensitive to it, so glucose uptake falls and blood glucose stays high. This insulin resistance is why diet and exercise, which restore sensitivity, are the first treatments.

questions.stem: What is the role of the hypothalamus in thermoregulation?

options.text: It passes on the core temperature measured by thermoreceptors in the skin to the effectors.
It generates heat itself whenever the blood flowing through it becomes too cold.
It monitors blood temperature and coordinates the responses of the effectors.
It secretes thyroxin directly into the blood to raise the metabolic rate.

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus contains thermoreceptors that measure the temperature of the blood flowing through it and also receives impulses from peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin. It compares these with the set point and sends nerve impulses to effectors and hormonal signals via the pituitary gland.

questions.stem: How does vasodilation of the arterioles in the skin lower body temperature?

options.text: More blood flows through the capillaries near the surface, so more heat is lost to the air.
The blood vessels move closer to the surface of the skin, so heat escapes more easily.
Warm blood at the surface is cooled by the cold sweat that lies on top of the skin.
The capillaries contract their walls to squeeze warm blood towards the surface.

questions.explanation: Relaxation of smooth muscle in the arteriole walls widens them, so a greater volume of warm blood passes through the capillary beds close to the skin surface, where heat is transferred to the surroundings by radiation, conduction and convection.

questions.stem: Which change would do most to reduce a middle-aged adult's risk of developing type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Beginning insulin injections before any symptoms appear.
Reducing body fat through diet and regular physical activity.
Avoiding the viral infections thought to trigger loss of beta cells.
Taking enzyme supplements that digest glucose in the blood.

questions.explanation: Obesity, a diet rich in sugar and fat, and inactivity are the main modifiable risk factors for type 2 diabetes because they reduce the sensitivity of target cells to insulin. Losing fat and exercising restore sensitivity, so this is the prevention the guide expects.

questions.stem: A person moves to a cold climate. After several weeks their resting metabolic rate has risen and they produce more heat even when not shivering. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The pituitary gland is secreting thyroxin, which acts as quickly as a nerve impulse.
The hypothalamus has started to produce extra heat itself as the blood cools.
A thicker layer of white fat is making extra ATP, and the ATP is released as heat.
More thyroxin is being secreted, raising the rate of cell respiration.

questions.stem: On a hot, very humid day a runner sweats heavily, but their body temperature keeps rising. Why is sweating less effective in these conditions?

options.text: The sweat produced is warmer than usual, so it cannot chill the skin as it runs off.
Little of the sweat evaporates, so little latent heat is taken from the skin.
Humid air stops the blood vessels from moving up to the surface of the skin.
Sweat cools mainly as it drips off, and humid air makes it drip slowly.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes osmoregulation from excretion?

options.text: Osmoregulation removes surplus water; excretion removes surplus solutes of every other kind.
Osmoregulation is carried out by the kidneys; excretion includes egestion of faeces by the gut.
Osmoregulation regulates the concentration of urea; excretion removes water from the body in urine.
Osmoregulation controls blood osmotic concentration; excretion removes metabolic waste.

questions.stem: Which statement about ultrafiltration in the glomerulus is correct?

options.text: Only urea and other toxins pass into Bowman's capsule, while glucose is retained in the blood.
Glucose, urea and salts all pass into Bowman's capsule, but plasma proteins do not.
Water and solutes enter Bowman's capsule by osmosis and diffusion down gradients.
The filtrate is almost all excreted as urine after small changes in the tubule.

questions.explanation: The glomerular filter (fenestrated capillary wall, basement membrane and podocyte slits) discriminates by size only. High blood pressure forces water and all small solutes through; blood cells and plasma proteins are retained, so the filtrate is plasma minus its proteins.

questions.stem: How does the loop of Henle make it possible for the kidney to produce concentrated urine?

options.text: Its ascending limb actively transports water out of the filtrate and into the tiny blood vessels of the medulla.
It absorbs sodium ions into the filtrate so that the urine leaving the loop is already highly concentrated.
Its cells actively pump water into the collecting ducts, from which the blood then reabsorbs it directly.
Its ascending limb pumps sodium ions into the medulla, so water leaves the collecting ducts by osmosis.

questions.stem: After drinking a litre of water, a person produces a large volume of dilute urine within an hour. What has happened in the cells of the collecting ducts?

options.text: Aquaporin genes have been switched off, so no new water channels are being made for the membrane.
More ADH has been secreted, and ADH increases the volume of urine that the ducts must release.
Aquaporins have been withdrawn into vesicles, so the membrane is far less permeable to water.
The duct cells sensed the dilute blood themselves and stopped pumping water inward.
